evidence_text: When the number of dimensions in the problem is large, PDEs and numerical integrals become intractable. In these cases Monte Carlo methods often give better results.

evidence_text: In these cases Monte Carlo methods often give better results. For simpler situations, simulation is not the better solution because it is very time-consuming and computationally intensive.
mechanism: While Monte Carlo methods are effective for complex problems, their computational intensity makes them less suitable for simpler situations where other methods are more efficient.

evidence_text: Monte Carlo methods can deal with derivatives which have path dependent payoffs in a fairly straightforward manner. Finite Difference (PDE) solvers struggle with path dependence.
mechanism: Path dependence introduces complexities that are more easily handled by simulation-based methods like Monte Carlo, while finite difference methods face difficulties in accurately capturing the history-dependent nature of the payoffs.

evidence_text: Post crisis, banks will make various “valuation adjustments” - collectively XVA - when assessing the value of derivative contracts that they have entered into. The purpose of these is twofold: primarily to hedge for possible losses due to the other parties' failures to pay amounts due on the derivative contracts (credit valuation adjustment); but also to determine (and hedge) the amount of capital required under the bank capital adequacy rules.
mechanism: Regulatory changes and increased risk awareness post-crisis necessitate valuation adjustments to account for potential losses and capital requirements.
